title: POC Weekly Sync - Model selection & pinning
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest perf numbers from the pilot, decide on a model to pin for staging canary, and confirm rollback/fallback strategies. Customer prefers pinning to a quantized 13B variant but is concerned about p90 latency and hallucination rate. Redwood AE/SE to send pinned config and perf spreadsheet; customer to run additional 1k samples and share logs.
topics: model catalog comparison and quantization tradeoffs
action_items: Maya Chen - Share pinned model config, quantization profile, and perf spreadsheet (due: 2025-09-03)
Sara Patel - Run additional 1k sample queries on staging and share logs + failure cases (due: 2025-09-08)
Liam O'Connor - Prepare canary rollout runbook and rollback steps, include API call examples (due: 2025-09-04)
David Liu - Confirm SSO / SAML test window for private deployment (due: 2025-09-05)
next_steps: Redwood to send pinned model JSON + perf sheet
Customer to run extra sample set and share results
Follow-up security Q&A doc to be reviewed by customer
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-01 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya, Liam (Redwood) -- Sara, David, Carlos (NorthBridge)

[00:00] Maya: Hey team, thanks for joining. Quick check — everyone can hear me?
[00:06] Sara: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:08] David: Yep.
[00:12] Maya: Great. Recap from last week, we pushed the RW-Base-13B-v2-quant candidate to staging and ran the initial 500-sample pass. Liam, do you want to summarize perf?
[00:25] Liam: Sure. So p50 we saw around 220ms on our dedicated cluster with batching at 8, p90 jumped to about 680ms for long context hits, token throughput about 120 t/s. Cost-wise the quantized profile cut token cost by ~32% versus the fp16 variant. There were a few outliers on p90 tied to very long KV-cache warmups and prefix reuse.
[00:47] Carlos: Sorry, when you say KV-cache warmups, do you mean the K-V cash or the prefix cache? We blew a few SLA windows last week because of long first-token latencies.
[00:54] Liam: Yeah — K-V cache, sorry, the auto prefix/K-V cache. That's where the first few earlier calls warmed the cache and subsequent requests were fast. The initial cold starts are the ones that bumped p90.
[01:08] Sara: On quality our internal evals — the hallucination rate for the quantized 13B seemed slightly higher on clinical domain prompts (roughly +2.5% vs the full-precision run). But latency improvements look promising.
[01:20] Maya: Right, and that tradeoff is exactly what we wanted to discuss — pinning to a quantized 13B for the pilot to save cost vs sticking with the 7B fast model for tighter latency SLAs.
[01:33] David: Can you remind us the names in the Redwood catalog we tested? I lost track — some of them are similar.
[01:39] Liam: We tested three variants: RW-Fast-7B-q4, RW-Base-13B-v2-quant, and RW-Instruction-70B-lite (the latter on a smaller slice for cost sim). The 70B had best quality but cost and latency were prohibitive for real-time features.
[01:56] Sara: The 7B had lower hallucination but we hit timeout thresholds on some of our longer context cases especially when the prompt includes long patient notes.
[02:08] Maya: So options: A) pin to RW-Base-13B-v2-quant for cost and decent quality, B) pin to RW-Fast-7B-q4 for latency-first path, or C) use smart routing so we route by policy — low-latency routes to 7B, complex/long-context to 13B.
[02:27] Carlos: Smart routing sounds ideal but more operational overhead. Also worried about consistent results between model variants — we can't have two models giving different triage outcomes.
[02:36] Liam: Totally — that's where version pinning plus rollout policies help. We can pin a single model version for the API route used by the front-end, and for edge cases you can configure a fallback route to the other variant. If inconsistency is a concern we can do A/B with a deterministic post-check step to reconcile outputs.
[02:54] Sara: For the POC success criteria we listed: 95% of requests under 500ms p90 and hallucination delta <1.5% vs our oracle. None of the configs today meet both.
[03:05] Maya: Understood. One pragmatic path is to pin 13B quant for the pilot, but set canary traffic to 10% and have automatic fallback to 7B for requests hitting the latency SLO. That gives you cost savings and a safety net.
[03:20] David: How does the fallback work? Is it synchronous (blocking) or async? We can't have double billing or double responses.
[03:26] Liam: It's synchronous from the platform perspective — request is evaluated against policy; if latency thresholds or error rates spike, the router sends to the fallback model. We don't double-run by default; we only reroute failed or slow requests. There's also an option for shadowing where you duplicate traffic for analysis but that costs more.
[03:42] Carlos: Shadowing we will avoid for now.
[03:45] Sara: Can you pinpoint what caused those hallucination deltas on clinical prompts? Any pattern?
[03:50] Liam: Most of the hallucinations were in long context merges where the quantization slightly impacted token probability ordering on rare medical terms. We're seeing it on low-frequency entities and detailed medication instructions.
[04:05] Maya: So two mitigation levers: increase the quantization profile (less aggressive q4-to-q5) which raises cost, or do targeted prompt engineering and retrieval augmentation to reduce hallucination triggers.
[04:16] Sara: Retrieval augmentation is feasible — we can add structured patient facts. But that will change our prompt footprint and possibly latency.
[04:23] David: On pinning semantics — once we pin a model version, how do rollbacks work? If we deploy v2 and see regressions, how quickly can we roll back?
[04:31] Liam: You can rollback instantly to the previous pinned version. In Dedicated/Private you control rollout windows; in Hosted we provide canary + quick rollback via the Console. We keep model versions immutable and keep adherence to the previous config so you can go back within minutes.
[04:47] Maya: We also support automatic fallback policies that can trigger when model-specific error rates or latency exceed thresholds. So even without a rollback you can divert traffic.
[04:56] Carlos: Does the platform keep audit logs for these rollouts? We need to show change history for compliance.
[05:01] Liam: Yes — audit logs show who changed the pinned version, the timestamp, and the rollout percentage. For Private you can send logs to your SIEM via syslog or S3.
[05:12] Sara: Security check — will the quantized model run in our VPC for Private deployment with KMS keys for encryption? We have to ensure PHI never leaves our tenancy.
[05:22] Maya: For Private deployments yes, you can run the runtime in your VPC and we integrate with KMS/HSM. In hosted mode we offer encryption-at-rest and redwood-managed keys or customer-managed keys with limited key access. We will share the security doc after the call.
[05:36] David: Great. Back to pinning decision — are you leaning a recommendation?
[05:40] Liam: From a technical tradeoff lens, pin RW-Base-13B-v2-quant to start — it meets most quality targets and lowers cost. Enable a 10% canary and a latency-based fallback to RW-Fast-7B-q4 for requests with predicted long contexts. Also set automated alert at 1% increase in hallucination or 20% spike in p90.
[06:03] Carlos: I like that. One question — if we fallback, do we log both responses for later comparison?
[06:08] Liam: We can enable logging for both only in shadow mode. In fallback mode we log the chosen path and the pre-fallback metrics; we don't compute the alternate response unless you opt into shadowing.
[06:20] Sara: Ok. For the canary run, what telemetry will you need from us to validate hallucination delta? Raw responses or redacted annotations?
[06:28] Maya: Redacted responses plus a small set of golden prompts annotated by your clinicians will be enough. We'll compute the delta offline and present a summary table.
[06:38] David: Any perf tuning we should try before pinning? You mentioned batching at 8 — what about dynamic batching or prefilling KV cache?
[06:45] Liam: We recommend request coalescing and warm-up jobs to prefill the KV cache for common prefixes. We can also tune the batch window — lowering it reduces latency but can affect throughput. We'll share recommended autoscaling and batching configs in the perf sheet.
[06:59] Maya: Quick note — in the perf runs there were some transcription glitches in the earlier spreadsheet, I fixed the headings; sending updated one with better p90 bucket breakdown.
[07:08] Sara: Thanks. Anything on SLOs for Dedicated vs Hosted? We may shift to Dedicated if we need guaranteed throughput.
[07:15] Liam: Dedicated gives SLA-backed latency and reserved GPU pools; Hosted is faster to iterate. For the POC, hosted with pinned model plus reserved burst capacity should be enough. If you see consistent QPS > X we'll engage Dedicated. We'll add that threshold to the doc.
[07:29] Carlos: How long should the canary run be to consider it representative? A week?
[07:33] Maya: Typically 3-7 days with daily sampling of telemetry — but since you have clinical peak windows, we'd align canary to include one full peak cycle. So plan for 7 days.
[07:43] David: Ok. Let's map next steps — send pinned config, perf sheet, run additional 1k samples, and prepare canary runbook.
[07:52] Maya: Yep. We'll send the pinned JSON and the perf spreadsheet by Thursday.
[07:56] Sara: We'll aim to finish the 1k runs by next Monday and share logs.
[08:00] Carlos: Scheduling — canary target 2025-09-10 as Maya mentioned.
[08:05] Liam: I'll draft the rollback steps and the Console screenshots for the runbook.
[08:09] Maya: Anything else — security doc? We'll attach that in the follow-up email.
[08:13] David: No other items. Thank you.
[08:16] Maya: Great, thanks everyone. End.

Notes: Transcript shows occasional auto-caption errors (K-V as K-V cash), speaker labels are accurate except where noted.
